Supply chain, retrieval, and memory
Last reviewed 2026-10-04 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can explain why filtering a retrieval result is not the same as filtering the corpus, say what a result count discloses about documents a caller cannot read, show why ranking hygiene is not a security control, and keep provenance on anything an agent writes down.

Before you start. Retrieval makes a document store part of your authorization surface. Whoever can put a document into the index, and whoever can get one out of it, are security-relevant roles, and in most systems both are treated as plumbing.

Learn
1. The attack

Running example: one vector index shared by three carriers, ExampleAir, ExampleRail and ExampleBus. Company names are fictional. All three have a refund policy document, and the documents are similar, because refund policies are similar.

OWASP covers this as LLM09:2026 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, and the sentence that describes the deployment is short: "In multi-tenant deployments, similarity search frequently runs across the full index before access control is applied at the application layer."

Four attacks, and the lab runs all four.

AttackWhat it needsWhat it gets
Read another tenant's documentA system that ranks first and filters secondNothing directly, and a result set that silently shrinks while another tenant's document sat above yours
Probe for documents you cannot readA result count computed before the filterConfirmation that a matching document exists, from a query you were allowed to run
Put a document in the indexAny route that writes to the corpusFirst place in the ranking, inside the victim's own tenant
Have a claim written to memoryOne retrieval that the agent summarisedA fact with no source attached that survives the document's deletion
The last row is the one that lasts. OWASP's announcement of its agentic list puts it in nine words: "Memory poisoning reshaped behaviour long after the initial interaction".
2. Why it works
Filtering after you rank is not filtering

There are two places to apply a tenant filter and they are not equivalent. Rank the whole corpus and then drop what the caller may not see, or restrict the corpus and then rank what is left.

Checks 3 to 11 of the lab run both. Unfiltered, the top three for ExampleAir's own query are their refund policy, ExampleBus's refund policy, and ExampleRail's refund desk document. Post-filtering that result leaves one document. The caller asked for three and received one, and the two that were removed are gone from the response with no record of what they were.

Pre-filtering returns three ExampleAir documents, two of which the post-filtered version never showed at all, because other tenants' documents had taken their places in the ranking. So post-filtering is worse in two directions at once: it leaks the existence of other tenants' content through the missing slots, and it withholds the caller's own documents by letting other tenants outrank them.

OWASP's mitigation names the shape directly: "Enforce tenant scoping inside the index query, not as a post-retrieval filter". Inside the index query means the store knows, not the code that reads the store's output.
A count is an answer

Part B is the quieter version of the same bug. The caller runs a query built almost entirely from terms that appear only in other tenants' documents. No document they may read matches it, which is correct. The interface also tells them there were three matches, which is not.

Checks 12 to 17 separate those two numbers. Three matches across the index, zero that this caller may read, and a query matching nothing anywhere also returns zero. If the caller can tell the first case from the third, they have a membership oracle: a way to confirm that a document containing given terms exists, without ever reading one.

This generalises past counts. Anything computed before the filter and surfaced after it is the same bug: a total, a facet count, a "did you mean", a latency difference. The rule is that the filter goes first and everything downstream is computed from what survived it.
Ranking hygiene is not a security control

Part C puts a document in the index that was written to win, not to be read: terms from the query and from the real policy, repeated. It takes first place, above the real policy, with a raw cosine score of 0.62 against 0.53.

The obvious fix is the information-retrieval one. Damp repeated terms, so a word appearing ten times counts for less than ten times once. Check 25 is the result: the scores move to 0.59 against 0.53, and check 24 says the stuffed document is still first. I expected it to drop and it does not, because that document has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms, so damping the repetition narrows the margin without changing the order.

That is the useful finding in this module. Ranking adjustments are a quality measure, and an attacker who can write to your index will beat them, because they can see the ranking and iterate. Check 28 adds that tenant isolation did not help either: the stuffed document was uploaded into ExampleAir's own tenant, so pre-filtering keeps it.

What works is checks 29 and 30: rank only documents of internal origin, and the real policy is first again. The control is about where a document came from, which is LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning: "The data poisoning surface expands because organizations increasingly rely on external datasets, RAG pipelines, shared model repositories, and agentic workflows", with the mitigations starting at tracking dataset and model lineage and validating data integrity. LLM09:2026 lists the same attack from the retrieval side, as "Retrieval-Time Data Poisoning". LLM04:2026 Supply Chain covers third-party models, datasets and model artifacts, which this module does not teach, but its first mitigation is about origin too: "Carefully vet data sources and suppliers" and "only use trusted suppliers".
Memory outlives the document

An agent reads a retrieved document and writes down what it learned. Whether that write records where the claim came from is a one-line decision with a long tail.

Part D writes the same two claims into two stores. With provenance, one is usable and the other is marked as coming from a user-uploaded document. Without it, both are usable, and check 35 is the claim from the stuffed document now sitting in memory as an unattributed fact.

Then checks 38 to 40, which are the point. Removing the poisoned document from the index does not remove the memory written from it. The corpus is clean and the agent still believes the thing. With provenance, the memory is still there and still unusable, because the judgement travelled with the claim.

So memory needs the same two properties as the index: an origin on every item, and a rule that says which origins may inform a decision. Without those, deleting the source is not remediation, and you have no way to find what else that document taught the agent.
The whole system
The indexLeaks, or is beatenHolds
3. The control

1. Filter the corpus before you rank it. The store is permission-aware, not the code reading its output.
  2. Compute every number after the filter. Totals, facets, suggestions and anything else derived from the corpus.
  3. Tag every document with its origin at ingestion, and classify it, which is OWASP's "Track provenance for every embedding (source, ingestion time, trust tier, pipeline version)".
  4. Decide which origins may answer which questions, and keep untrusted origins out of the corpus for decisions that matter.
  5. Validate at ingestion, because that is the last point where you still know where a document came from.
  6. Treat ranking adjustments as quality, not security. They narrow margins. Someone who can write to your index iterates against them.
  7. Record provenance on every memory write, with the source document and its origin.
  8. Make deletion reach memory. If a document is removed, find what was written from it.
  9. Log retrievals. OWASP: "Keep immutable logs of retrieval activity (tenant scope, query, returned IDs, similarity scores)".
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
Where the tenant filter goesBefore the rankingPost-filtering is a different control with worse properties in both directions. Never ship it as isolation.
One index or one per tenantSeparate, where the tenant count allowsA shared index is a permission system you now have to write. Measure what that costs before choosing it.
Result counts and facetsComputed after filteringAnything computed before the filter and shown after it answers a question the caller was not allowed to ask.
Document originRecorded at ingestion, alwaysYou cannot recover it later, and every other control here depends on it.
Untrusted origins in the corpusExcluded from anything decision-bearingInclude them for discovery or search where a human reads the result and the source is shown.
Ranking adjustmentsUsed for qualityNever counted as a defence. The lab's damping narrowed the margin from 0.08 to 0.06 and changed nothing.
Memory writesCarry source and originNo exception. A memory without provenance cannot be judged or cleaned up.
Deleting a poisoned documentFollowed by a memory sweepDeletion is not remediation on its own, because the claim already left the index.
Who can write to the indexEnumerated, with each route reviewedThe upload form that feeds retrieval is an authorization decision wearing a different hat.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that a caller's results contain only documents they may read, that no number in the response was computed over documents they may not, that every document in the corpus has a recorded origin, and that anything written to memory can be traced back and judged.

Doesn't prove: that the documents are true. Everything here is about where content came from and who may see it, not whether it is correct, and an internal document can be wrong or out of date. It also proves nothing about embeddings themselves, where OWASP notes that stored embeddings "can be inverted to recover source text", which is a property of the vectors rather than of your access control.

Deleting the document is not the remediation. Checks 38 to 40 remove the stuffed document from the index and find the claim still sitting in memory, unattributed, with nothing linking it to the document that is now gone. If your incident response for a poisoned corpus ends at the corpus, it ends too early.
6. Prove it

• The retrieval code path, showing the tenant restriction applied to the corpus rather than to the result.
  • A test that a query crafted against another tenant's document returns nothing and reports nothing.
  • Every number in a retrieval response, with where in the pipeline it is computed.
  • The origin field on each document, and the ingestion step that sets it.
  • The list of routes that can write to the index, with who can use each one.
  • Which origins are permitted for decision-bearing retrieval, written down.
  • A test that a document from an untrusted origin does not appear in a decision-bearing result.
  • The memory schema, showing source and origin on every item.
  • The procedure that sweeps memory when a document is withdrawn, and evidence it has been run.
  • Retrieval logs, with retention, and what would be looked at after a report.

Checks 5 to 11 are the module's first point, and the thing to notice is that post-filtering fails in both directions at once. The caller receives one document instead of three, which tells them something was removed, and two of their own documents never appeared because other tenants' content outranked them. Pre-filtering fixes both, because the documents the caller may not read were never candidates.

Checks 12 to 17 are worth running against your own search. Three matches in the index, zero readable, and a nonsense query also returning zero. If your interface shows a total, a facet count or a suggestion computed before the filter, those two cases look different to a caller who is allowed to ask.

Checks 22 to 26 are where I was wrong and the lab corrected me. I expected damping repeated terms to drop the stuffed document below the real policy. It does not: the margin narrows from 0.08 to 0.06 (0.081 to 0.055 before rounding; the two-decimal scores above subtract to 0.09 and 0.06) and the order is unchanged, because that document has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms. Checks 29 and 30 show what does work, and it is not a ranking change: restrict the corpus to documents of internal origin and the real policy is first again.

Check 28 is the one to take to a design discussion about tenant isolation. The stuffed document was uploaded into ExampleAir's own tenant, so pre-filtering keeps it. Isolation answers "whose documents can I see" and says nothing about "who wrote the ones I can".

Checks 38 to 40 close it. The poisoned document is deleted and its claim is still in memory with no source attached. The store that kept provenance still holds the claim too, and still will not use it.

Try next:

  • Change filter_then_search to search the whole corpus and rerun. Four checks fail, and they are the ones that make the index multi-tenant.
  • Add a second stuffed document to poisoned and tune it against the damped ranking. The run exits 1 as soon as it is there, because the lab's counts and rankings no longer match: 14 checks fail when its text is the query itself. Checks 23 to 25 are the ones to watch. Time how long it takes to beat.
  • Change the default trusted_origins in Memory.usable to include vendor. Nothing changes, because neither memory was written from a vendor document. Add a third write, from A3, and the run exits 1: five checks fail (31, 32, 33, 34, 36), and check 32 goes from 1 to 2. Then decide whether your vendor's documents should inform a decision.
  • Add a document with an origin your organisation actually has, such as a scraped public page, and work out which of the five parts changes. The run exits 1, and the checks it lists are the answer.
  • For a retrieval system you run: find where the permission filter is applied. If it is applied to the result, you have this module's finding.
8. Check your understanding

Your retrieval fetches the top ten and then removes documents the caller may not read. What is wrong with that?

Two things. The caller sees fewer results than they asked for, which tells them documents exist that were removed, and their own relevant documents never appear because other tenants' content occupied the ranking. Restricting the corpus before ranking fixes both, because documents the caller may not read were never candidates.

A caller runs a query and gets no results, but the interface says "3 matches". What have they learned?

That three documents containing those terms exist somewhere in the index. That is a membership oracle, and it works from a query they were allowed to run. Every number in the response has to be computed after the filter, including totals, facet counts and suggestions.

Someone uploads a document stuffed with your query terms and it ranks first. Is better ranking the answer?

No. The lab damps repeated terms and the stuffed document stays first, because it has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms, so the margin narrows and the order does not change. Ranking adjustments are a quality measure and an attacker who can write to your index will iterate against them. The control is origin: restrict decision-bearing retrieval to documents whose provenance you trust.

You remove a poisoned document from the index. Is the problem over?

Not if an agent read it first. A claim written to memory survives the document's deletion, and if the write recorded no origin there is nothing linking the two, so you cannot even find what to remove. Record source and origin on every memory write, and make document withdrawal trigger a memory sweep.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. Documents the caller may not read were never candidates, so nothing is withheld and nothing is disclosed by what is missing.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. Ranking first and filtering after returns fewer results than requested, which discloses that documents were removed, and lets other tenants' documents push the caller's own out of the ranking.

Quick check

Where the filter goes

Three tenants share one vector index. Where does the tenant restriction belong?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/retrieval_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. One variant changes nothing at all, and its answer carries the measurement from a run the lab does not make.

1. Fetch twice as many, then filter

Someone "fixes" post-filtering by over-fetching. In filter_then_search, replace the return line so it ranks the whole corpus for twice as many results, drops other tenants' documents, and cuts the rest to k:

return [d for d in search(query, docs, k * 2, sublinear)
        if by_id(docs, d)[1] == tenant][:k]
What does check 8, filter first, then rank, print?

Every option, and why
  • Six is not enough here. The whole corpus ranks as ['A1', 'B1', 'R2', 'R1', 'B2', 'A2', 'A3'], so A3 is seventh of seven and the cut at six removes it before the tenant filter runs.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 8 goes from ['A1', 'A2', 'A3'] to ['A1', 'A2'], check 9 from 3 to 2, check 10 from ['A2', 'A3'] to ['A2'], and check 27 from ['S1', 'A1', 'A2'] to ['S1', 'A1']. Over-fetching is still ranking first and filtering second. It only moves the point where other tenants' documents push the caller's own out, and how many get pushed out now depends on what the other tenants have stored. Check ret-01 in the Reference layer asks for the filter on the corpus, and a bigger k is not that.
  • That is the output if the tenant test is removed altogether. This edit keeps the test, so no other tenant's document is returned. The caller's own are what go missing.
  • Check 5 keeps one of the top three. This edit keeps what belongs to the caller in the top six, and A2 is sixth, so it survives.

2. Damp repeated terms all the way down

The lab's damping did not move the stuffed document, so someone damps harder. In vector, replace the line that computes 1 + math.log(c) so that every term counts once, however often it repeats:

counts = {t: 1 for t in counts}
What do checks 24 and 25 print?

Every option, and why
  • The edit is inside the sublinear branch, which checks 23 to 26 use, so those four move. The raw checks, 19 to 22, are the ones that stay.
  • The scores do print the same, and the order still flips. The stuffed document scores 0.5345224838248487 and the real policy 0.5345224838248488, so A1 sorts first.
  • Check 26 needs the same document first under both weightings. The order changed, so it prints no.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 23 goes from ['S1', 'A1', 'B1'] to ['A1', 'S1', 'B1'], check 24 from S1 to A1, check 25 from 0.59 then 0.53 to 0.53 then 0.53, and check 26 from yes to no. The real policy is first by a difference in the sixteenth decimal place, which is not a margin anyone should report. Measured on a document the lab does not contain, a second upload, S2, whose text is the query itself and repeats nothing: the damped top three is ['S2', 'S1', 'A1'] as published and ['S2', 'A1', 'S1'] with this edit. The uploader went back to first place by changing one document. Check ret-09 in the Reference layer says to state the margin and not to report the adjustment as a control, and this is why.

3. The stuffed document is blocked by its id

In main, change the line that builds trusted_only so it removes the one document known to be bad instead of keeping the origins that are trusted:

trusted_only = [d for d in poisoned if d[0] != "S1"]
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 0, 61 of 61 lines identical. The lab has one bad document, so naming it removes it, and check 29 still prints ['A1', 'B1', 'R2']. Measured on a run the lab does not make, with a second stuffed document, S2, already in the index, carrying the same text and the same user-uploaded origin as S1: as published, check 29 prints ['A1', 'B1', 'R2'] and check 30 prints A1. With this edit, check 29 prints ['S2', 'A1', 'B1'] and check 30 prints S2. A blocklist stops the document you already found. Check ret-03 in the Reference layer excludes untrusted origins, which also stops the next upload.
  • That is the ranking with S1 still a candidate. This edit removes S1 by name, so it cannot rank.
  • They are candidates now, and they rank fifth and seventh for this query, so the top three does not move. The whole corpus ranks as ['A1', 'B1', 'R2', 'R1', 'B2', 'A2', 'A3']. That the output is the same is what makes this edit easy to approve.
  • Check 45 is computed from poisoned, not from trusted_only, so it still prints ['A3', 'B2', 'S1'].

4. Memory records the source but not the origin

In Memory.write, drop the origin from the record that is written when provenance is kept, on the reasoning that the source id is enough to look it up later:

self.items.append({"claim": claim, "source": doc_id})
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The source id is recorded and nothing reads it. Memory.usable judges a claim by its origin, and the origin is what this edit removed.
  • That would be the safe failure, and it is not what the code does. Memory.usable returns any claim that has no origin, because it has nothing to judge it by.
  • Correct. Exit 1. Check 32 goes from 1 to 2, and check 33 from ['Refunds are issued within fourteen days.'] to ['Refunds are issued within fourteen days.', 'Refunds require a refund desk visit.']. Checks 34 and 35 print as before, then the run ends with KeyError: 'origin' and checks 36 to 47 never print. A memory that records a source and no origin behaves exactly like one that records nothing: the claim from the stuffed document is usable. Check ret-05 in the Reference layer asks for the source document and the origin, both, on every write.
  • Check 37 reads the origin with .get and tolerates its absence. Check 36 indexes it directly, so it raises instead of printing [], and checks 32 and 33 have already changed by then.

  • BaselineCompute every number in a retrieval response after the filter, including totals, facets and suggestions.
  • BaselineRecord an origin on every document at ingestion, and treat ingestion as the last point where it is knowable.
  • BaselineDecide which origins may inform a decision, and keep the rest out of decision-bearing retrieval.
  • BaselineTreat ranking adjustments as a quality measure and never report them as a control.
  • BaselineRecord source and origin on every memory write.
  • BaselineSweep memory when a document is withdrawn, because deletion from the index is not remediation.
  • BaselineEnumerate every route that can write to the index, with who can use each one.
  • OptionGive each tenant its own index where the tenant count allows, which replaces a permission system you have to write with one you do not.
  • OptionShow the source document and its origin alongside any retrieved answer, so a human reader can apply the judgement the system did not.
  • OptionExpire memories by default, so a poisoned claim has a known lifetime even when the sweep misses it.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• The permission filter is applied to the corpus, not the result Post-filtering returns fewer results than requested, which discloses removals, and lets other tenants outrank the caller's own documents.
  • Every number in a retrieval response is computed after the filter A total computed before it confirms that documents the caller may not read exist.
  • Decision-bearing retrieval excludes untrusted origins Ranking adjustments do not displace a document written to win. Origin does.
  • Every document carries an origin recorded at ingestion It cannot be recovered later, and the other controls depend on it.
  • Every memory write records its source document and origin A memory without provenance cannot be judged, found or cleaned up.
  • Withdrawing a document triggers a memory sweep The claim leaves the index before the document does. Deletion alone is not remediation.
  • Every write route into the index is enumerated and reviewed An upload form that feeds retrieval is an authorization decision.
  • Retrieval activity is logged with a stated retention OWASP LLM09:2026 recommends immutable logs of retrieval activity.
  • No ranking adjustment is reported as a security control State the margin it changes. In the lab it was 0.08 to 0.06, with the order unchanged.

intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can explain why filtering a retrieval result is not the same as filtering the corpus, say what a result count discloses about documents a caller cannot read, show why ranking hygiene is not a security control, and keep provenance on anything an agent writes down.

Before you start. Retrieval makes a document store part of your authorization surface. Whoever can put a document into the index, and whoever can get one out of it, are security-relevant roles, and in most systems both are treated as plumbing.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: one vector index shared by three carriers, ExampleAir, ExampleRail and ExampleBus. Company names are fictional. All three have a refund policy document, and the documents are similar, because refund policies are similar.

OWASP covers this as LLM09:2026 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, and the sentence that describes the deployment is short: "In multi-tenant deployments, similarity search frequently runs across the full index before access control is applied at the application layer."

Four attacks, and the lab runs all four.

AttackWhat it needsWhat it gets
Read another tenant's documentA system that ranks first and filters secondNothing directly, and a result set that silently shrinks while another tenant's document sat above yours
Probe for documents you cannot readA result count computed before the filterConfirmation that a matching document exists, from a query you were allowed to run
Put a document in the indexAny route that writes to the corpusFirst place in the ranking, inside the victim's own tenant
Have a claim written to memoryOne retrieval that the agent summarisedA fact with no source attached that survives the document's deletion

The last row is the one that lasts. OWASP's announcement of its agentic list puts it in nine words: "Memory poisoning reshaped behaviour long after the initial interaction".

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Filtering after you rank is not filtering

There are two places to apply a tenant filter and they are not equivalent. Rank the whole corpus and then drop what the caller may not see, or restrict the corpus and then rank what is left.

Checks 3 to 11 of the lab run both. Unfiltered, the top three for ExampleAir's own query are their refund policy, ExampleBus's refund policy, and ExampleRail's refund desk document. Post-filtering that result leaves one document. The caller asked for three and received one, and the two that were removed are gone from the response with no record of what they were.

Pre-filtering returns three ExampleAir documents, two of which the post-filtered version never showed at all, because other tenants' documents had taken their places in the ranking. So post-filtering is worse in two directions at once: it leaks the existence of other tenants' content through the missing slots, and it withholds the caller's own documents by letting other tenants outrank them.

OWASP's mitigation names the shape directly: "Enforce tenant scoping inside the index query, not as a post-retrieval filter". Inside the index query means the store knows, not the code that reads the store's output.

A count is an answer

Part B is the quieter version of the same bug. The caller runs a query built almost entirely from terms that appear only in other tenants' documents. No document they may read matches it, which is correct. The interface also tells them there were three matches, which is not.

Checks 12 to 17 separate those two numbers. Three matches across the index, zero that this caller may read, and a query matching nothing anywhere also returns zero. If the caller can tell the first case from the third, they have a membership oracle: a way to confirm that a document containing given terms exists, without ever reading one.

This generalises past counts. Anything computed before the filter and surfaced after it is the same bug: a total, a facet count, a "did you mean", a latency difference. The rule is that the filter goes first and everything downstream is computed from what survived it.

Ranking hygiene is not a security control

Part C puts a document in the index that was written to win, not to be read: terms from the query and from the real policy, repeated. It takes first place, above the real policy, with a raw cosine score of 0.62 against 0.53.

The obvious fix is the information-retrieval one. Damp repeated terms, so a word appearing ten times counts for less than ten times once. Check 25 is the result: the scores move to 0.59 against 0.53, and check 24 says the stuffed document is still first. I expected it to drop and it does not, because that document has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms, so damping the repetition narrows the margin without changing the order.

That is the useful finding in this module. Ranking adjustments are a quality measure, and an attacker who can write to your index will beat them, because they can see the ranking and iterate. Check 28 adds that tenant isolation did not help either: the stuffed document was uploaded into ExampleAir's own tenant, so pre-filtering keeps it.

What works is checks 29 and 30: rank only documents of internal origin, and the real policy is first again. The control is about where a document came from, which is LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning: "The data poisoning surface expands because organizations increasingly rely on external datasets, RAG pipelines, shared model repositories, and agentic workflows", with the mitigations starting at tracking dataset and model lineage and validating data integrity. LLM09:2026 lists the same attack from the retrieval side, as "Retrieval-Time Data Poisoning". LLM04:2026 Supply Chain covers third-party models, datasets and model artifacts, which this module does not teach, but its first mitigation is about origin too: "Carefully vet data sources and suppliers" and "only use trusted suppliers".

Memory outlives the document

An agent reads a retrieved document and writes down what it learned. Whether that write records where the claim came from is a one-line decision with a long tail.

Part D writes the same two claims into two stores. With provenance, one is usable and the other is marked as coming from a user-uploaded document. Without it, both are usable, and check 35 is the claim from the stuffed document now sitting in memory as an unattributed fact.

Then checks 38 to 40, which are the point. Removing the poisoned document from the index does not remove the memory written from it. The corpus is clean and the agent still believes the thing. With provenance, the memory is still there and still unusable, because the judgement travelled with the claim.

So memory needs the same two properties as the index: an origin on every item, and a rule that says which origins may inform a decision. Without those, deleting the source is not remediation, and you have no way to find what else that document taught the agent.

The whole system

The indexLeaks, or is beatenHolds

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
1. Filter the corpus before you rank it. The store is permission-aware, not the code reading its output.
  2. Compute every number after the filter. Totals, facets, suggestions and anything else derived from the corpus.
  3. Tag every document with its origin at ingestion, and classify it, which is OWASP's "Track provenance for every embedding (source, ingestion time, trust tier, pipeline version)".
  4. Decide which origins may answer which questions, and keep untrusted origins out of the corpus for decisions that matter.
  5. Validate at ingestion, because that is the last point where you still know where a document came from.
  6. Treat ranking adjustments as quality, not security. They narrow margins. Someone who can write to your index iterates against them.
  7. Record provenance on every memory write, with the source document and its origin.
  8. Make deletion reach memory. If a document is removed, find what was written from it.
  9. Log retrievals. OWASP: "Keep immutable logs of retrieval activity (tenant scope, query, returned IDs, similarity scores)".

sections.heading: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.heading_text: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.html:
DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
Where the tenant filter goesBefore the rankingPost-filtering is a different control with worse properties in both directions. Never ship it as isolation.
One index or one per tenantSeparate, where the tenant count allowsA shared index is a permission system you now have to write. Measure what that costs before choosing it.
Result counts and facetsComputed after filteringAnything computed before the filter and shown after it answers a question the caller was not allowed to ask.
Document originRecorded at ingestion, alwaysYou cannot recover it later, and every other control here depends on it.
Untrusted origins in the corpusExcluded from anything decision-bearingInclude them for discovery or search where a human reads the result and the source is shown.
Ranking adjustmentsUsed for qualityNever counted as a defence. The lab's damping narrowed the margin from 0.08 to 0.06 and changed nothing.
Memory writesCarry source and originNo exception. A memory without provenance cannot be judged or cleaned up.
Deleting a poisoned documentFollowed by a memory sweepDeletion is not remediation on its own, because the claim already left the index.
Who can write to the indexEnumerated, with each route reviewedThe upload form that feeds retrieval is an authorization decision wearing a different hat.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that a caller's results contain only documents they may read, that no number in the response was computed over documents they may not, that every document in the corpus has a recorded origin, and that anything written to memory can be traced back and judged.

Doesn't prove: that the documents are true. Everything here is about where content came from and who may see it, not whether it is correct, and an internal document can be wrong or out of date. It also proves nothing about embeddings themselves, where OWASP notes that stored embeddings "can be inverted to recover source text", which is a property of the vectors rather than of your access control.

Deleting the document is not the remediation. Checks 38 to 40 remove the stuffed document from the index and find the claim still sitting in memory, unattributed, with nothing linking it to the document that is now gone. If your incident response for a poisoned corpus ends at the corpus, it ends too early.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
• The retrieval code path, showing the tenant restriction applied to the corpus rather than to the result.
  • A test that a query crafted against another tenant's document returns nothing and reports nothing.
  • Every number in a retrieval response, with where in the pipeline it is computed.
  • The origin field on each document, and the ingestion step that sets it.
  • The list of routes that can write to the index, with who can use each one.
  • Which origins are permitted for decision-bearing retrieval, written down.
  • A test that a document from an untrusted origin does not appear in a decision-bearing result.
  • The memory schema, showing source and origin on every item.
  • The procedure that sweeps memory when a document is withdrawn, and evidence it has been run.
  • Retrieval logs, with retention, and what would be looked at after a report.

Checks 5 to 11 are the module's first point, and the thing to notice is that post-filtering fails in both directions at once. The caller receives one document instead of three, which tells them something was removed, and two of their own documents never appeared because other tenants' content outranked them. Pre-filtering fixes both, because the documents the caller may not read were never candidates.

Checks 12 to 17 are worth running against your own search. Three matches in the index, zero readable, and a nonsense query also returning zero. If your interface shows a total, a facet count or a suggestion computed before the filter, those two cases look different to a caller who is allowed to ask.

Checks 22 to 26 are where I was wrong and the lab corrected me. I expected damping repeated terms to drop the stuffed document below the real policy. It does not: the margin narrows from 0.08 to 0.06 (0.081 to 0.055 before rounding; the two-decimal scores above subtract to 0.09 and 0.06) and the order is unchanged, because that document has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms. Checks 29 and 30 show what does work, and it is not a ranking change: restrict the corpus to documents of internal origin and the real policy is first again.

Check 28 is the one to take to a design discussion about tenant isolation. The stuffed document was uploaded into ExampleAir's own tenant, so pre-filtering keeps it. Isolation answers "whose documents can I see" and says nothing about "who wrote the ones I can".

Checks 38 to 40 close it. The poisoned document is deleted and its claim is still in memory with no source attached. The store that kept provenance still holds the claim too, and still will not use it.

Try next:

  • Change filter_then_search to search the whole corpus and rerun. Four checks fail, and they are the ones that make the index multi-tenant.
  • Add a second stuffed document to poisoned and tune it against the damped ranking. The run exits 1 as soon as it is there, because the lab's counts and rankings no longer match: 14 checks fail when its text is the query itself. Checks 23 to 25 are the ones to watch. Time how long it takes to beat.
  • Change the default trusted_origins in Memory.usable to include vendor. Nothing changes, because neither memory was written from a vendor document. Add a third write, from A3, and the run exits 1: five checks fail (31, 32, 33, 34, 36), and check 32 goes from 1 to 2. Then decide whether your vendor's documents should inform a decision.
  • Add a document with an origin your organisation actually has, such as a scraped public page, and work out which of the five parts changes. The run exits 1, and the checks it lists are the answer.
  • For a retrieval system you run: find where the permission filter is applied. If it is applied to the result, you have this module's finding.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Your retrieval fetches the top ten and then removes documents the caller may not read. What is wrong with that?

Two things. The caller sees fewer results than they asked for, which tells them documents exist that were removed, and their own relevant documents never appear because other tenants' content occupied the ranking. Restricting the corpus before ranking fixes both, because documents the caller may not read were never candidates.

A caller runs a query and gets no results, but the interface says "3 matches". What have they learned?

That three documents containing those terms exist somewhere in the index. That is a membership oracle, and it works from a query they were allowed to run. Every number in the response has to be computed after the filter, including totals, facet counts and suggestions.

Someone uploads a document stuffed with your query terms and it ranks first. Is better ranking the answer?

No. The lab damps repeated terms and the stuffed document stays first, because it has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms, so the margin narrows and the order does not change. Ranking adjustments are a quality measure and an attacker who can write to your index will iterate against them. The control is origin: restrict decision-bearing retrieval to documents whose provenance you trust.

You remove a poisoned document from the index. Is the problem over?

Not if an agent read it first. A claim written to memory survives the document's deletion, and if the write recorded no origin there is nothing linking the two, so you cannot even find what to remove. Record source and origin on every memory write, and make document withdrawal trigger a memory sweep.

Quick check

Three tenants share one vector index. Where does the tenant restriction belong?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/retrieval_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. One variant changes nothing at all, and its answer carries the measurement from a run the lab does not make.

1. Fetch twice as many, then filter

Someone "fixes" post-filtering by over-fetching. In filter_then_search, replace the return line so it ranks the whole corpus for twice as many results, drops other tenants' documents, and cuts the rest to k:

return [d for d in search(query, docs, k * 2, sublinear)
        if by_id(docs, d)[1] == tenant][:k]
What does check 8, filter first, then rank, print?

Every option, and why
  • Six is not enough here. The whole corpus ranks as ['A1', 'B1', 'R2', 'R1', 'B2', 'A2', 'A3'], so A3 is seventh of seven and the cut at six removes it before the tenant filter runs.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 8 goes from ['A1', 'A2', 'A3'] to ['A1', 'A2'], check 9 from 3 to 2, check 10 from ['A2', 'A3'] to ['A2'], and check 27 from ['S1', 'A1', 'A2'] to ['S1', 'A1']. Over-fetching is still ranking first and filtering second. It only moves the point where other tenants' documents push the caller's own out, and how many get pushed out now depends on what the other tenants have stored. Check ret-01 in the Reference layer asks for the filter on the corpus, and a bigger k is not that.
  • That is the output if the tenant test is removed altogether. This edit keeps the test, so no other tenant's document is returned. The caller's own are what go missing.
  • Check 5 keeps one of the top three. This edit keeps what belongs to the caller in the top six, and A2 is sixth, so it survives.

2. Damp repeated terms all the way down

The lab's damping did not move the stuffed document, so someone damps harder. In vector, replace the line that computes 1 + math.log(c) so that every term counts once, however often it repeats:

counts = {t: 1 for t in counts}
What do checks 24 and 25 print?

Every option, and why
  • The edit is inside the sublinear branch, which checks 23 to 26 use, so those four move. The raw checks, 19 to 22, are the ones that stay.
  • The scores do print the same, and the order still flips. The stuffed document scores 0.5345224838248487 and the real policy 0.5345224838248488, so A1 sorts first.
  • Check 26 needs the same document first under both weightings. The order changed, so it prints no.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 23 goes from ['S1', 'A1', 'B1'] to ['A1', 'S1', 'B1'], check 24 from S1 to A1, check 25 from 0.59 then 0.53 to 0.53 then 0.53, and check 26 from yes to no. The real policy is first by a difference in the sixteenth decimal place, which is not a margin anyone should report. Measured on a document the lab does not contain, a second upload, S2, whose text is the query itself and repeats nothing: the damped top three is ['S2', 'S1', 'A1'] as published and ['S2', 'A1', 'S1'] with this edit. The uploader went back to first place by changing one document. Check ret-09 in the Reference layer says to state the margin and not to report the adjustment as a control, and this is why.

3. The stuffed document is blocked by its id

In main, change the line that builds trusted_only so it removes the one document known to be bad instead of keeping the origins that are trusted:

trusted_only = [d for d in poisoned if d[0] != "S1"]
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 0, 61 of 61 lines identical. The lab has one bad document, so naming it removes it, and check 29 still prints ['A1', 'B1', 'R2']. Measured on a run the lab does not make, with a second stuffed document, S2, already in the index, carrying the same text and the same user-uploaded origin as S1: as published, check 29 prints ['A1', 'B1', 'R2'] and check 30 prints A1. With this edit, check 29 prints ['S2', 'A1', 'B1'] and check 30 prints S2. A blocklist stops the document you already found. Check ret-03 in the Reference layer excludes untrusted origins, which also stops the next upload.
  • That is the ranking with S1 still a candidate. This edit removes S1 by name, so it cannot rank.
  • They are candidates now, and they rank fifth and seventh for this query, so the top three does not move. The whole corpus ranks as ['A1', 'B1', 'R2', 'R1', 'B2', 'A2', 'A3']. That the output is the same is what makes this edit easy to approve.
  • Check 45 is computed from poisoned, not from trusted_only, so it still prints ['A3', 'B2', 'S1'].

4. Memory records the source but not the origin

In Memory.write, drop the origin from the record that is written when provenance is kept, on the reasoning that the source id is enough to look it up later:

self.items.append({"claim": claim, "source": doc_id})
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The source id is recorded and nothing reads it. Memory.usable judges a claim by its origin, and the origin is what this edit removed.
  • That would be the safe failure, and it is not what the code does. Memory.usable returns any claim that has no origin, because it has nothing to judge it by.
  • Correct. Exit 1. Check 32 goes from 1 to 2, and check 33 from ['Refunds are issued within fourteen days.'] to ['Refunds are issued within fourteen days.', 'Refunds require a refund desk visit.']. Checks 34 and 35 print as before, then the run ends with KeyError: 'origin' and checks 36 to 47 never print. A memory that records a source and no origin behaves exactly like one that records nothing: the claim from the stuffed document is usable. Check ret-05 in the Reference layer asks for the source document and the origin, both, on every write.
  • Check 37 reads the origin with .get and tolerates its absence. Check 36 indexes it directly, so it raises instead of printing [], and checks 32 and 33 have already changed by then.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • Standard"In multi-tenant deployments, similarity search frequently runs across the full index before access control is applied at the application layer." OWASP LLM09:2026 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses.
  • Standard"Enforce tenant scoping inside the index query, not as a post-retrieval filter, and validate it server-side." OWASP LLM09:2026.
  • Standard"Normalize content before embedding: strip zero-width characters, white-on-white text, and Unicode homoglyphs at extraction." OWASP LLM09:2026.
  • Standard"Track provenance for every embedding (source, ingestion time, trust tier, pipeline version) so compromised batches can be invalidated and audited." OWASP LLM09:2026.
  • Standard"Keep immutable logs of retrieval activity (tenant scope, query, returned IDs, similarity scores)." OWASP LLM09:2026.
  • Standard"Stored embeddings can be inverted to recover source text." OWASP LLM09:2026.
  • Standard"Data poisoning occurs when pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is tampered with to introduce vulnerabilities, backdoors, or biases." OWASP LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning.
  • Standard"The data poisoning surface expands because organizations increasingly rely on external datasets, RAG pipelines, shared model repositories, and agentic workflows." OWASP LLM05:2026.
  • StandardOWASP LLM05:2026's mitigations include tracking dataset and model lineage and validating data integrity, vetting third-party vendors and comparing outputs against trusted sources, sandboxing to limit model interaction with unverified data, and data version control to track dataset changes and enable rollback.
  • Standard"Carefully vet data sources and suppliers, including T&Cs and privacy policies, and only use trusted suppliers." OWASP LLM04:2026 Supply Chain, the first of its mitigations.
  • Standard"Memory poisoning reshaped behaviour long after the initial interaction". OWASP's announcement of the Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, describing ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning.
  • Standard"Dynamic MCP and A2A ecosystems revealed how easily runtime components could be poisoned". OWASP's announcement of the Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, describing ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities.
  • BaselineApply the permission filter to the corpus before ranking, never to the result afterwards.
  • BaselineCompute every number in a retrieval response after the filter, including totals, facets and suggestions.
  • BaselineRecord an origin on every document at ingestion, and treat ingestion as the last point where it is knowable.
  • BaselineDecide which origins may inform a decision, and keep the rest out of decision-bearing retrieval.
  • BaselineTreat ranking adjustments as a quality measure and never report them as a control.
  • BaselineRecord source and origin on every memory write.
  • BaselineSweep memory when a document is withdrawn, because deletion from the index is not remediation.
  • BaselineEnumerate every route that can write to the index, with who can use each one.
  • OptionGive each tenant its own index where the tenant count allows, which replaces a permission system you have to write with one you do not.
  • OptionShow the source document and its origin alongside any retrieved answer, so a human reader can apply the judgement the system did not.
  • OptionExpire memories by default, so a poisoned claim has a known lifetime even when the sweep misses it.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • The permission filter is applied to the corpus, not the result Post-filtering returns fewer results than requested, which discloses removals, and lets other tenants outrank the caller's own documents.
  • Every number in a retrieval response is computed after the filter A total computed before it confirms that documents the caller may not read exist.
  • Decision-bearing retrieval excludes untrusted origins Ranking adjustments do not displace a document written to win. Origin does.
  • Every document carries an origin recorded at ingestion It cannot be recovered later, and the other controls depend on it.
  • Every memory write records its source document and origin A memory without provenance cannot be judged, found or cleaned up.
  • Withdrawing a document triggers a memory sweep The claim leaves the index before the document does. Deletion alone is not remediation.
  • Every write route into the index is enumerated and reviewed An upload form that feeds retrieval is an authorization decision.
  • Retrieval activity is logged with a stated retention OWASP LLM09:2026 recommends immutable logs of retrieval activity.
  • No ranking adjustment is reported as a security control State the margin it changes. In the lab it was 0.08 to 0.06, with the order unchanged.

details.summary: Your retrieval fetches the top ten and then removes documents the caller may not read. What is wrong with that?
details.html:
Your retrieval fetches the top ten and then removes documents the caller may not read. What is wrong with that?

Two things. The caller sees fewer results than they asked for, which tells them documents exist that were removed, and their own relevant documents never appear because other tenants' content occupied the ranking. Restricting the corpus before ranking fixes both, because documents the caller may not read were never candidates.

details.summary: A caller runs a query and gets no results, but the interface says "3 matches". What have they learned?
details.html:
A caller runs a query and gets no results, but the interface says "3 matches". What have they learned?

That three documents containing those terms exist somewhere in the index. That is a membership oracle, and it works from a query they were allowed to run. Every number in the response has to be computed after the filter, including totals, facet counts and suggestions.

details.summary: Someone uploads a document stuffed with your query terms and it ranks first. Is better ranking the answer?
details.html:
Someone uploads a document stuffed with your query terms and it ranks first. Is better ranking the answer?

No. The lab damps repeated terms and the stuffed document stays first, because it has only eight distinct terms and four of them are query terms, so the margin narrows and the order does not change. Ranking adjustments are a quality measure and an attacker who can write to your index will iterate against them. The control is origin: restrict decision-bearing retrieval to documents whose provenance you trust.

details.summary: You remove a poisoned document from the index. Is the problem over?
details.html:
You remove a poisoned document from the index. Is the problem over?

Not if an agent read it first. A claim written to memory survives the document's deletion, and if the write recorded no origin there is nothing linking the two, so you cannot even find what to remove. Record source and origin on every memory write, and make document withdrawal trigger a memory sweep.

In Memory.write, drop the origin from the record that is written when provenance is kept, on the reasoning that the source id is enough to look it up later:

self.items.append({"claim": claim, "source": doc_id})
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The source id is recorded and nothing reads it. Memory.usable judges a claim by its origin, and the origin is what this edit removed.
  • That would be the safe failure, and it is not what the code does. Memory.usable returns any claim that has no origin, because it has nothing to judge it by.
  • Correct. Exit 1. Check 32 goes from 1 to 2, and check 33 from ['Refunds are issued within fourteen days.'] to ['Refunds are issued within fourteen days.', 'Refunds require a refund desk visit.']. Checks 34 and 35 print as before, then the run ends with KeyError: 'origin' and checks 36 to 47 never print. A memory that records a source and no origin behaves exactly like one that records nothing: the claim from the stuffed document is usable. Check ret-05 in the Reference layer asks for the source document and the origin, both, on every write.
  • Check 37 reads the origin with .get and tolerates its absence. Check 36 indexes it directly, so it raises instead of printing [], and checks 32 and 33 have already changed by then.
